outputs.final_proof:
\begin{proof}
We establish the equality by proving the two inclusions.

If $f(x)\in(2x)$, then $f(x)=2xg(x)$ for some $g(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Thus
\[
f(x)=2(xg(x))=x(2g(x)),
\]
so $f(x)\in(2)$ and $f(x)\in(x)$. Therefore $(2x)\subseteq(2)\cap(x)$.

Conversely, let $p(x)\in(2)\cap(x)$. Write $p(x)=2h(x)$ with $h(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Since $p(x)\in(x)$, its constant coefficient is zero. Comparing constant coefficients in $p(x)=2h(x)$ gives $2h(0)=0$, hence $h(0)=0$ because $\mathbb{Z}$ is an integral domain. Consequently, $h(x)=xq(x)$ for some $q(x)\in\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Therefore
\[
p(x)=2h(x)=2xq(x)\in(2x),
\]
so $(2)\cap(x)\subseteq(2x)$.

The two inclusions imply $(2)\cap(x)=(2x)$.
\end{proof}
